## Paper

## Abstract

Assembly line biosynthesis creates numerous structurally diverse natural products using a
common modular synthetic strategy. The collinearity between the architectures of modular
polyketide synthases (PKS) and the structures of their polyketide products would seem to
render these biosynthetic machineries excellent platforms for designer biosynthesis, yet
reliable strategies to reprogram these assembly lines without diminishing their activities have
not been identified. Here, as a best practice for PKS engineering, we demonstrate the
reprogramming of the mediomycin PKS without significant loss of productivity. Using in
vitro CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing followed by heterologous expression, we reconstruct an
inaccessible drug lead of the fibrinogen receptor, tetrafibricin, at 82 ± 3 mg/L yield, retaining
26% productivity after five-step module editing using an evolution-supported cut site,
downstream of the acyltransferase domain. A macrocyclic aminopolyol is also accessed
through thioesterase swapping. These results pave the way toward the rational
reprogramming of PKSs to access desired complex organic molecules.

---

## Introduction

Modular polyketide synthases (PKSs) are multidomain enzyme complexes that biosynthesize a
wide variety of polyketide natural products, including the clinically important medicines
erythromycin, tacrolimus (FK506), and ivermectin (a semi-synthetic derivative of avermectin)1.
The reaction cycle of a PKS module is equivalent to that of the metazoan fatty acid synthase
(FAS)2-4 - a carbon building block that is passed from an acyltransferase (AT) domain to an acyl
carrier protein (ACP) domain and a growing acyl chain that is bound to a ketosynthase (KS)
domain are fused to generate an elongated chain that can be processed by accompanying
ketoreductase (KR), dehydratase (DH), and enoylreductase (ER) domains. However, the
multimodular nature of PKS assembly lines enables differential processing of each intermediate5-
8. In theory, PKSs can be engineered to access designer polyketides; however, in practice9-14 the
efficient (i.e., retaining production titre) and flexible reprogramming of PKSs is challenging due
to our limited understanding of domain-domain interactions and substrate recognition10,15-17.
The PKS module is the set of domains responsible for one round of chain extension and processing.
It was originally defined with an upstream KS and a downstream ACP18. However, studies have
shown that KSs can act as gatekeepers that select between intermediates bound to the upstream
ACP19-22, and that interactions between these two domains are important23,24. Additionally, our
previous evolutionary analysis of aminopolyol PKSs revealed that KSs genetically co-migrate with
upstream processing enzymes19 and we expanded this idea to other types of PKSs (Supplementary
Fig. 1). This co-migration is apparent in modular PKSs both with and without embedded ATs,
known as cis-AT and trans-AT PKSs19,25. How often AT domains co-migrate with neighbouring
enzymatic domains in cis-AT PKSs is likely related to the chemistry they perform together. Sets
of processing enzymes+ACP+KS that incorporate an -methyl substituent in a stereocontrolled
manner collaborate with methylmalonyl-specific upstream ATs21. KSs that extend polyketides with
ethylmalonyl extender units collaborate with ethylmalonyl-specific downstream ATs26. How well
such sets of enzymatic domains tolerate AT swaps is the subject of active investigation27. While
the genetic co-migration of processing enzymes and KSs within cis-AT PKSs was studied by
comparing related aminopolyol PKSs, the co-migration of its predominantly malonyl-specific AT
domains could not be studied due to gene conversion, which overwrites their evolutionary
history19,28. Thus, to reprogram aminopolyol PKSs, we evaluated two alternative strategies to
determine which was superior, AT+processing enzymes+ACP+KS units (exchange unit or “XU”)
or processing enzymes+ACP+KS+AT units (“XUA”). “XU” was originally introduced in the
context of nonribosomal peptide synthetase engineering29 and later adopted for PKS engineering14.
Because KS and AT are structurally connected, engineering modular PKSs by XUA-based module
editing might be a reasonable strategy (Fig. 1)30-32.

Here, we demonstrate the skeletal editing of aminopolyol polyketide structures through PKS
reprogramming. Using a previously established heterologous expression system for mediomycin
biosynthetic gene cluster19 as a platform, an artificial PKS was engineered through successive
multidomain manipulations to produce tetrafibricin, a fibrinogen receptor inhibitor33,34, with a
yield of 104 ± 4 µM (82 ± 3 mg/L) [mean ± s.e.m. (n = 3), the same applies below], demonstrating
the most complex and efficient multistep PKS engineering achieved to date to the best of our
knowledge. Furthermore, we produced an artificial macrolactone using the ACP-TE co-
transplantation strategy developed in this study.

---

## Results

Reconstructing the carbon scaffold of tetrafibricin
Tetrafibricin is an aminopolyol polyketide with potent fibrinogen receptor inhibition activity that
was first isolated in 199333,34. Subsequent attempts to obtain tetrafibricin from the producing strain
have been unsuccessful19, dropping this non-peptidyl antiplatelet drug candidate out of further
development. Interestingly, the “producer” strain, S. neyagawaensis NR0557, instead produces a
larger polyketide, neotetrafibricin. Based on the domain architecture of the neotetrafibricin PKS,
misdocking between tfbORF5 and tfbORF9, premature hydrolysis by TE, or spontaneous
degradation during the isolation process may have led to tetrafibricin formation. As an alternative
approach, tetrafibricin has been targeted by chemical synthesis. While many fragment syntheses
have been reported, none has yet yielded the final natural product35.

We previously reported that the structural diversification of aminopolyols is naturally driven by
the recombination of the genes encoding PKSs19. Thus, we envisioned performing similar
recombinations in the lab to transform the mediomycin PKS (medPKS) into a tetrafibricin-
producing PKS (Supplementary Fig. 2a). To this end, the mediomycin biosynthetic gene cluster
was cloned into a bacterial artificial chromosome (BAC) for in vitro gene editing using
CRISPR/Cas9 (Supplementary Fig. 2b)13. The heterologous expression of this BAC in
Streptomyces lividans TK23 ΔredD–X, an engineered host lacking the undecylprodigiosin
biosynthetic gene cluster, was demonstrated in our previous work to enable the production of
clethramycin and desulfoclethramycin (guanidinylated mediomycin and desulfomediomycin)19.
When this work was initiated, we measured a combined yield of these polyketides of 533 ± 6 µM
(635 ± 7 mg/L). Given that this level of productivity was sufficiently high, we selected this host
for subsequent experiments. The guanidino group is not hydrolysed to an amine to provide
mediomycin and desulfomediomycin since medX, the gene encoding the amidinohydrolase, was
not originally included in the BAC because it is located outside of the mediomycin biosynthetic
gene cluster36.

We first attempted to swap XUA7 and XUA9 within medPKS, as in a natural recombination event
that occurred in the evolution of the aminopolyol PKSs19. In this campaign, XUA9 was first
duplicated (PKSv1), but then the doubling was resolved (PKSv2), which had the benefit of
minimizing opportunities for internal recombination. The cut site for the XUA boundary was set
C-terminal to the first tyrosine of the conserved LPTY(A/P)FQ(H/R)xRYWL motif in the last half
of the post-AT linker,37 referred to as PAL227 (Supplementary Figs. 2b and 2d). This evolution-
guided engineering19 preserves the interactions between KS, the upstream ACP, and the upstream
processing enzymes. The genes encoding the engineered assembly line, PKSv1, were expressed in
S. lividans TK23 ΔredD–X19. The anticipated products (Fig. 1b) 1a + 1b were generated at a
combined yield of 436 ± 55 µM (524 ± 66 mg/L), 82% that of clethramycin and
desulfoclethramycin (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 3a). Next, the downstream XUA9 was
replaced by XUA7 to create PKSv2 (Fig. 1a), which generated 2a + 2b at a combined yield of 298
± 33 µM (347 ± 38 mg/L) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 3a). The structures of 1b and 2b were
confirmed by HR-MS analyses (Supplementary Table 1 and Supplementary Figs. 10–24) and a
series of NMR analyses (Supplementary Fig. 4, Supplementary Tables 2 and 3) (see also
Supplementary Figs. 25–55 for 1D and 2D NMR spectral data).

In the third step, we sought to trim the carboxy end of the polyketide product. It has been well-
documented that such a truncation can be obtained through the appropriate positioning of a
thioesterase (TE) domain38. Thus, we first positioned the mediomycin TE (medTE) downstream
of the ACP domain of XUA19 to create PKSv3_medTE (Supplementary Fig. 2c and 2f). However,
only a trace amount of the expected product 3 was detected by mass spectrometry (Supplementary
Fig. 5). Introduction of the pikromycin TE (pikTE) was also attempted (Supplementary Fig. 5);
however, PKSv3_pikTAE (Supplementary Fig. 2c and 2f) only generated 3 at a yield of 59 ± 7 µM
(49 ± 6 mg/L), 20% that of 2a + 2b. Inspired by the recent ACP-centric view of PKS modules,
we
hypothesized that the natural ACP cognate of medTE might be necessary for efficient TE-catalysed
hydrolysis. With the ACP+TE didomain from the medPKS positioned downstream of the KR
domain of XUA19 (Supplementary Fig. 1e), PKSv3 (Fig. 1a) generated 3 at a yield of 249 ± 15
µM (205 ± 12 mg/L), 84% that of 2a + 2b (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 3b). The sulfonated
analogue of 3 was not observed.

In the fourth step, XUA11 was removed from PKSv3 (Fig. 1a). The resulting PKSv4 generated 4
at a yield of 265 ± 26 µM (211 ± 21 mg/L), 106% that of 3 (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 3b).
Finally, a copy of XUA4 was inserted downstream of XUA2 (Fig. 1a). The resulting PKSv5
generated 5 at a yield of 140 ± 2 µM (115 ± 2 mg/L) (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Fig. 3b). The
yield of 5 was 53% that of 4.

XUA vs. XU strategy
At this stage, we had successfully created the polyketide skeleton of tetrafibricin through five steps
of PKS engineering using the XUA strategy. We then compared the XUA strategy with the XU
strategy, which employs a domain set with KS as the most downstream domain (AT+processing
enzymes+ACP+KS) (Fig. 2a). The XU strategy has been effectively applied in recent years to
modify several cis-AT PKSs and has been shown to be more effective than swapping using the
traditional module boundary9,12,14,39.

For Steps 1, 2, 4 and 5, we generated PKSv1_IXU, PKSv2_XU, PKSv4_XU and PKSv5_XU from
medPKS, PKSv1, PKSv3 and PKSv4, respectively (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 2f), using the
region 10 aa downstream of the GTNAH motif located at the C-terminal of the KS domain as the
cut site for the XU strategy. This cut site was employed and shown to work in a previous study40.
Step 3, which involves the migration of ACP-TE units, is not relevant to the comparison of the
XUA and XU strategies.

As a result, PKSv1_XU, PKSv2_XU, PKSv4_XU, and PKSv5_XU showed 93%, 82%, 59%, and
51% yields of PKSv1, PKSv2, PKSv4, and PKSv5, respectively (Fig. 2c). The differences in yield
between PKSv4 and PKSv4_XU (p < 0.001) and PKSv5 and PKSv5_XU (p = 0.002) were
statistically significant, while those between PKSv1 and PKSv1_XU (p = 0.383) and PKSv2 and
PKSv2_XU (p = 0.484) were not. These findings suggest that, at least in the context of
aminopolyol PKS engineering, the XUA strategy appears more robust against productivity loss.

Production of tetrafibricin
The PKSv5 product 5 differs from tetrafibricin in its guanidino group. To convert this group to an
amine, we aimed to co-express an amidinohydrolase gene from the aminopolyol producing strains
with PKSv5. To identify a promiscuous amidinohydrolase, tfbX1, tfbX2, ecoX, and medX were
each co-expressed with PKSv4 (Supplementary Fig. 6a). As TfbX1 and EcoX efficiently converted
4 to 7, tfbX1 and ecoX were each expressed with PKSv5, and both of them successfully converted
5 to tetrafibricin. The more efficient combination, tfbX1 and PKSv5, produced tetrafibricin at a
yield of 104 ± 4 µM (82 ± 3 mg/L) (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 6b). The yield of tetrafibricin
was 75% that of 5, demonstrating the efficiency of TfbX1. Notably, ecoX co-expression with
PKSv3 or PKSv4 gave 6 (227 ± 15 µM; 178 ± 12 mg/L) or 7 (188 ± 39 µM; 142 ± 29 mg/L),
respectively (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 6b), showcasing the promiscuity of EcoX. The
structures of 6, 7 and tetrafibricin were determined by HR-MS analyses (Supplementary Table 1)
and a series of NMR analyses (Supplementary Fig. 4, Supplementary Tables 4–6). Tetrafibricin
produced through module editing here showed potent fibrinogen receptor antagonistic activity, as
previously reported (see Supplementary Discussion).

Notably, a transformant carrying PKSv5, cultured before monospore isolation (see Methods),
generated 9 (Supplementary Fig. 7), a two-module-skipped version of 5. Co-expression of tfbX1
without isolating spores resulted in 10 (Supplementary Table 7) as the major product (tetrafibricin
was observed as a minor product). Plausibly, in vivo recombination between two direct repeat
regions encoding XUA4 (spanning 5,322 bp) occurred. On the other hand, we observed that the
productivity of 5 or tetrafibricin was not abolished even after a subculture, suggesting that the
recombination event occurs during transformation. Interestingly, we did not observe an equivalent
recombination for PKSv1, which possesses 2 copies of XUA9, for reasons that are unknown.

Production of an aminopolyol macrolide and its biological activity
Macrocyclic polyketides often exhibit potent bioactivities, as exemplified by clinical drugs such
as erythromycin and amphotericin. By applying the ACP+TE didomain transplantation strategy
that efficiently yielded 3, we further exploited TEs from other macrolactone PKS systems to
engineer an aminopolyol macrolide. We transplanted the ACP+TE didomains from the PKSs that
produce the macrocycles desertomycin and amphotericin for the ACP+TE didomain of medPKS
(Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 2f). Although the amphotericin ACP+TE transplant only provided
trace quantities of cyclic product 8, the desertomycin ACP+TE transplant, PKSv6, yielded 8 at 9.6
± 0.4 µM (11.5 ± 0.5 mg/L) (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 8). The ester moiety of 8 was observed
by NMR, confirming the production of an artificial 54-membered macrolide (Fig. 4c and
Supplementary Table 8). The desertomycin TE was also transplanted without its cognate ACP,
generating PKSv6(TE) (Fig. 4a), but the yield was half that of PKSv6 (5.1 ± 0.3 µM; 6.1 ± 0.4
mg/L) (Fig. 4b).

The antibacterial and cytotoxic activities of 8 were evaluated. This cyclized clethramycin did not
inhibit the growth of Micrococcus luteus and Staphylococcus aureus, while clethramycin showed
weak activity against both strains (IC for M. luteus was 32.1 µM, agreeing with a previous report)
50
(Supplementary Fig. 9Aa). Cytotoxicity was measured on T lymphoma Jurkat cells, human ovarian
adenocarcinoma SKOV-3 cells, and malignant pleural mesothelioma MESO-1 cells. Whereas
clethramycin showed cytotoxicity (IC 0.32, 6.0 and 20 µM, respectively) equivalent to that of
50
etoposide (0.28, 2.3 and 16 µM, respectively), 8 was only active against Jurkat cells and ~100-
times less potent (23 µM) (Supplementary Fig. 9b).

---

## Methods

Plasmids and bacterial strains
Plasmids and bacterial strains used in this study are listed in Supplementary Tables 9 and 10,
respectively.

The culturing procedures of bacterial strains followed our previous paper54. Specifically, the
growth of Escherichia coli strains DH5α and NEB10β (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA) used
Luria broth (LB), which contained (per L of deionized water) 10 g of tryptone, 5 g of yeast extract,
and 5 g of NaCl, and was adjusted to pH 7.5 following formulation. The corresponding solid
medium (LA) was prepared by supplementing LB with agar at 15 g/L. For the production of
engineered products, each transformant of Streptomyces lividans TK23 ΔredD-X was inoculated
into a 50-mL test tube containing 15 mL of seed medium, containing (per L of deionized water)
5 g of glucose, 15 g of soya flour, and 5 g of yeast extract; the cells were cultured with reciprocal
shaking at 320 rpm and 27°C for 2 days. A 375-μL aliquot of the resulting vegetative culture was
used to inoculate a 125-mL flask containing 15 mL of the production media. The production media
contained (per L of deionized water) 20 g of glycerol, 10 g of molasses, 5 g of casein, 1 g of
Polypepton, and 4 g of CaCO ; the pH was adjusted to 7.2 following formulation. The fermentation
3
cultures were grown on a rotary shaker at 180 rpm and 27°C for 6 days. For quantification or large-
scale preparation of the products, cells were grown under the same conditions in baffled 500-mL
flasks, each containing 100 mL of the production media.

In vitro module editing
The principle of in vitro module editing is originally described in ref. 6. In brief, a parent BAC
was digested in vitro by Cas9, and then a donor DNA was ligated by Gibson assembly.
sgRNAs (see Supplementary Data 1 for target sequences) were prepared using the EnGen sgRNA
Synthesis Kit, S. pyogenes (New England Biolabs), following the manufacturer’s instructions. The
Cas9 (New England Biolabs) reaction mixture containing the specific combination of a parent
BAC and sgRNAs (Supplementary Table 11) was incubated at 37°C for 120 min. The digested
BAC and the donor DNA (Supplementary Data 2) were subjected to Gibson assembly. After 50
min-incubation at 50°C, the ligated DNA (edited BAC) was recovered by
phenol/chloroform/isoamyl alcohol treatment followed by 2-propanol precipitation, then
transformed into E. coli NEB10β by electroporation. The transformants were selected on LA
containing 100 µg mL−1 ampicillin and 50 µg mL−1 kanamycin. The obtained plasmids were
further confirmed by PCR (Supplementary Data 1) and restriction digestion.

Cloning of amidinohydrolases
medX was amplified by PCR using the genomic DNA of S. blastmyceticus NBRC12747 as a
template. ecoX (AAX98207), tfbX1 (WP_190130807) and tfbX2 (WP_190128809) were
synthesized and cloned into pUC-GW-Kan by GENEWIZ (South Plainfield, NJ), which were used
as PCR templates. The primers used for PCR are listed in table S11. The PCR fragments were
subcloned into the XbaI-HindIII site of pKU565T_ermE*p.

Transformation of Streptomyces lividans TK23 ΔredD-X
The BACs and expression vectors for amidinohydrolases were introduced into S. lividans TK23
ΔredD-X by PEG-assisted protoplast transformation. Subsequently, the transformants carrying
pKU518med_PKSv5 were subjected to monospore isolation as follows. Mature spores were
harvested from transformants grown on SFM agar plates containing (per L of tap water) 20 g of
mannitol, 20 g of soya flour, and 20 g of agar. A dense spore suspension was serially diluted and
plated onto fresh SFM agar. Well-separated single colonies were then picked and patched to new
SFM agars for further analysis.

UHPLC/MS analysis of culture extract
One millilitre of culture broth was lyophilized and then extracted with 1 ml of methanol. Debris
were removed by centrifugation and the supernatant was filtrated through 0.22 µm PTFE
membrane to give an analytical sample for UHPLC. Analytical UHPLC and HR-ESI-MS (positive
mode) were performed using a ACQUITY UPLC System (Waters, Framingham, MA) in
conjunction with a ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (1.7 µm, 2.1 i.d. × 100 mm) (Waters), a
ACQUITY UPLC PDA eλ detector (Waters), and a XevoG2 ToF system (Waters). Mobile phase
A was water + 0.1% formic acid, and mobile phase B was acetonitrile + 0.1% formic acid. The
flow rate was 0.8 mL min−1, and the column temperature was kept at 55˚C by a column oven. The
gradient elution program was 5−100% B over 5 min and 100% B for 1 min. The isocratic elution
was performed by 37% B for clethramycin, desulfoclethramycin, 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b and 8, 17% B for
3, 4, 6 and 7, and 15% for 5, tetrafibricin, 9 and 10 (n=1 for each sample). Data acquisitions and
analyses were performed by using MassLynx V4.1 software (Waters). The standard curve for
clethramycin was obtained based on the peak area of UV chromatogram at 358 nm, and applied
for quantifying clethraymcin and the compounds sharing the same conjugated double bond system
with clethramycin (i.e. desulfoclethramycin, 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b and 8). Similarly, the standard curve
for tetrafibricin was obtained based on the peak area of UV chromatogram at 337 nm, and applied
for quantifying tetrafibricin and the compounds sharing the same conjugated double bond system
with tetrafibricin (i.e. 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10).

Isolation of compounds
Isolation of 1b
